In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''Schubert variety''' is a certain [[algebraic variety|subvariety]] of a [[Grassmannian]], <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math> of <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces of a vector space <math>V</math>, usually with [[Mathematical singularity|singular points]]. Like the Grassmannian, it is a kind of [[moduli space]], whose elements satisfy conditions giving lower bounds to the dimensions of the intersections of its elements  <math>w\subset V</math>, with the elements of a specified [[complete flag]]. Here <math>V</math> may be a vector space over an arbitrary [[Field (mathematics)|field]], but most commonly this taken to be either the real or the [[complex number]]s. 

A typical example is the set <math>X</math> of <math>2</math>-dimensional subspaces <math>w \subset V</math> of a 4-dimensional  space <math>V</math> that intersect a fixed (reference) 2-dimensional subspace  <math>V_2</math> nontrivially.
:<math>X \ =\ \{w\subset V \mid \dim(w)=2,\, \dim(w \cap V_2)\ge 1\}.</math>

Over the [[real number]] field, this can be pictured in usual ''xyz''-space as follows. Replacing subspaces with their corresponding projective spaces, and intersecting with an affine coordinate patch of <math>\mathbb{P}(V)</math>, we obtain an open subset ''X''° &sub; ''X''. This is isomorphic to the set of all lines ''L'' (not necessarily through the origin) which meet the ''x''-axis. Each such line ''L'' corresponds to a point of ''X''°, and continuously moving ''L'' in space (while keeping contact with the ''x''-axis) corresponds to a curve in ''X''°. Since there are three degrees of freedom in moving ''L'' (moving the point on the ''x''-axis, rotating, and tilting), ''X'' is a three-dimensional real [[algebraic variety]]. However, when ''L'' is equal to the ''x''-axis, it can be rotated or tilted around any point on the axis, and this excess of possible motions makes ''L'' a singular point of ''X''.

More generally, a Schubert variety in <math>\mathbf{Gr}_k(V)</math>  is defined by specifying the minimal dimension of intersection of a <math>k</math>-dimensional subspace <math>w\subset V</math> with each of the spaces in a fixed reference complete flag <math>V_1\subset V_2\subset \cdots \subset V_n=V</math>, where <math>\dim V_j=j</math>.  (In the example above, this would mean requiring certain intersections of the line ''L'' with the ''x''-axis and the ''xy''-plane.)

In even greater generality, given a [[Semisimple algebraic group|semisimple]] [[algebraic group]] <math>G</math> with a [[Borel subgroup]] <math>B</math> and a standard parabolic subgroup <math>P</math>, it is known that the [[homogeneous space]] <math>G/P</math>, which is an example of a [[flag variety]], consists of finitely many <math>B</math>-orbits, which may be parametrized by certain elements <math>w\in W</math> of the [[Weyl group]] <math>W</math>. The closure of the <math>B</math>-orbit associated to an element <math>w\in W</math> is denoted <math>X_{w}</math> and is called a Schubert variety in <math>G/P</math>. The classical case corresponds to <math>G=SL_n</math>, with <math>P=P_k</math>, the <math>k</math>th maximal parabolic subgroup of <math> SL_n</math>, so that <math>G/P = \mathbf{Gr}_k(\mathbf{C}^n)</math> is the Grassmannian of <math>k</math>-planes in <math> \mathbf{C}^n</math>.

== Significance ==
Schubert varieties form one of the most important and best studied classes of [[smooth scheme|singular algebraic varieties]]. A certain measure of singularity of Schubert varieties is provided by [[Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial]]s, which encode their local Goresky–MacPherson [[intersection cohomology]].

The algebras of regular functions on Schubert varieties have deep significance in [[algebraic combinatorics]] and are examples of [[algebra with a straightening law|algebras with a straightening law]]. (Co)homology of the Grassmannian, and more generally, of more general flag varieties, has a basis consisting of the (co)homology classes of Schubert varieties, or '''Schubert cycles'''. The study of the intersection theory on the Grassmannian was initiated by [[Hermann Schubert]] and continued by [[Hieronymus Georg Zeuthen|Zeuthen]] in the 19th century under the heading of [[enumerative geometry]]. This area was deemed by [[David Hilbert]] important enough to be included as the [[Hilbert's fifteenth problem|fifteenth]] of his celebrated [[Hilbert problems|23 problems]]. The study continued in the 20th century as part of the general development of [[algebraic topology]] and [[representation theory]], but accelerated in the 1990s beginning with the work of [[William Fulton (mathematician)|William Fulton]] on the [[degeneracy loci]] and [[Schubert polynomial]]s, following up on earlier investigations of [[Joseph Bernstein|Bernstein]]–[[Israel Gelfand|Gelfand]]–Gelfand and [[Demazure]] in representation theory in the 1970s, [[Alain Lascoux|Lascoux]] and [[Marcel-Paul Schützenberger|Schützenberger]] in combinatorics in the 1980s, and Fulton and MacPherson in [[intersection theory]] of singular algebraic varieties, also in the 1980s.
